title: Rabi' al-Awwal
hookLine: the month of the Prophet's birth and death, marked differently by different Muslims

cards: Someone asks the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, about fasting on Mondays. A practical question. His answer, kept in Sahih Muslim, isn't practical at all.
In paraphrase: that is the day I was born, and the day revelation came down to me. So he marked the day of his own birth, every week, with a fast.
Some Muslims recall that answer when a particular month comes round each year: Rabi' al-Awwal, the month tradition gives for his birth, and for his death.

teach.h: A BIRTH AND A DEATH IN ONE MONTH.
teach.b: The Qur'an never gives the date of his birth. The early biographies place it in Rabi' al-Awwal, and tradition places his death in the same month.

Al-Bukhari keeps a report that he died on a Monday, the day of the week he was born. The exact day of the month is remembered differently by different communities. Then the celebration, as those who keep it explain it.
Some Muslims mark his birth with a gathering called the mawlid, which you met back in year two. People recite the Qur'an, sing poems in his praise, tell the story of his life and share food.

teach.h: THE MAWLID: JOY AT A MERCY.
teach.b: They describe it as joy at a mercy, and point to surah al-Anbiya, in Pickthall's words: "We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples."
If Allah sent a mercy, they say, it's right to be glad of it, and they point to the Monday fast as his own way of marking the day.
Then the restraint, as those who hold back explain it. Other Muslims, and some scholars, hold that his birth shouldn't be set apart as a festival, because the Prophet and his companions didn't do so.
They keep the month like any other, and say their love for him is no less.
For them, the way to honor him is to follow his example every day, and they point to surah al-Ahzab: "Verily in the messenger of Allah ye have a good example."
Notice what both share. Nobody is arguing about whether to love him. They differ about how to show it.
Both say they're doing it for him.

how: Some Muslims mark the Prophet's birth in Rabi' al-Awwal with a mawlid gathering of Qur'an recitation, poetry in his praise, stories of his life and shared food; others, following scholars who hold it shouldn't be set apart as a festival, keep the month like any other and honor him by following his example.

o: the month tradition gives for the Prophet's birth and death
the month of the Hajj, when pilgrims go to Makkah
the month the Qur'an was first revealed to the Prophet

p: sent as a mercy for the peoples

s: the Qur'an gives the date of the Prophet's birth
it doesn't; the month comes from the early biographies and tradition.
in Sahih Muslim, he linked his Monday fast to his birth
that is the day I was born, and the day revelation came to me.
Muslims who don't celebrate the mawlid love him less
they differ about how to show love, not whether to love him.

games.q: someone asks the Prophet why he fasts on Mondays. what does he say?
o: it's the day I was born, and the day revelation came to me.
it's the easiest day of the week to fast.
because Ramadan began on a Monday.
games.why: in Sahih Muslim, he ties the Monday fast to his own birth and to the coming of revelation.

practice: Bring back one scene from his life you've met on this path, serving his family, tending sheep, weeping at his son's death, and hold it.
Then pick one part of his life you don't know yet, to read about this month in a sira, a biography. If you pray, you can send blessings on him as Muslims do when his name is said.

wordCard.voice: Rabi' al-Awwal. The month tradition gives for the Prophet's birth and his death, marked with a mawlid by some Muslims and kept like any other month by others. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the name of the month tradition gives for the Prophet's birth.

carryVoice: Your line: his month. Both sides say they do it for him. See you tomorrow.
